library-reef-food-web-limits: This model shows a few possible feeding connections, not every species or every meal on Guam’s reefs. Arrows point from food toward the eater to show energy transfer. Sunlight is an energy source, not an organism. Real food webs branch, change, include decomposers and can have other energy sources; this sunlit example leaves most of that out.
library-reef-food-web-light-1: Sunlight supplies energy for photosynthesis in this sunlit-ocean model.
library-reef-food-web-light-2: Sunlight is not food that a fish can swallow.
library-reef-food-web-producer-2: Many use light to make food.
library-reef-food-web-producer-3: Algae and some microbes on reef surfaces can use light to make food too.
library-reef-food-web-grazer-3: Draw the arrow from the food toward the eater.
library-reef-food-web-predator-1: A larger fish may eat a smaller fish.
library-reef-food-web-predator-3: This line shows one possibility, not a rule for every fish.
library-reef-food-web-branch-1: Many parrotfish graze on material on reef surfaces.
library-reef-food-web-branch-3: The film includes tiny living food; this is not a rule that every parrotfish eats large seaweed.
library-reef-food-web-branch-4: A web can have several paths rather than one straight chain.
library-reef-food-web-limits-1: Real reefs include many more organisms, including decomposers.
library-reef-food-web-limits-2: Our picture does not show every link or calculate what happens when an animal is removed.
library-water-journey-limits: These are possible changes, not a required circle or a weather forecast. Real water can stay in one store for a long time, take other routes, move in many places at once and pass through plants. Invisible water vapor is a gas; visible cloud droplets are liquid or ice. The drawing is not to scale and does not show safe drinking water.
library-water-journey-heat-1: Some liquid water becomes invisible water vapor.
library-water-journey-heat-2: The Sun supplies energy for much evaporation.
library-water-journey-heat-3: Not all the ocean turns into vapor at once.
library-water-journey-freeze-1: Liquid water can freeze into solid ice.
library-water-journey-freeze-2: Salty seawater freezes at a lower temperature than pure water.
library-water-journey-freeze-3: Our picture skips the temperature and time details.
library-water-journey-cool-1: When water vapor cools enough, it can condense into tiny liquid droplets.
library-water-journey-cool-2: Clouds contain tiny droplets, ice crystals or both; they are not bags of invisible gas.
library-water-journey-grow-1: Cloud particles can grow and fall.
library-water-journey-grow-2: In warm conditions, falling liquid drops are rain.
library-water-journey-grow-3: Clouds do not squeeze themselves like a sponge.
library-water-journey-warm-1: Cloud droplets can evaporate back into invisible water vapor.
library-water-journey-warm-2: Water can take many paths; a cloud does not have to become rain.
library-water-journey-soak-1: Some rain soaks into the ground through pores and cracks.
library-water-journey-soak-2: Some water stays near roots and some moves deeper.
library-water-journey-soak-3: Not every rock passes water at the same rate.
library-water-journey-runoff-1: Some water flows over the land toward streams and the sea.
library-water-journey-runoff-2: The path depends on the land, rain and surfaces it meets.
library-water-journey-flow-1: Some groundwater moves toward the ocean.
library-water-journey-flow-2: Other water remains stored or is taken up by plants.
library-water-journey-flow-3: This step is not a claim that groundwater flows instantly.
library-water-journey-melt-1: Solid ice can melt into liquid water.
library-water-journey-melt-2: Freezing and melting change water’s state, not its chemical identity.
library-water-journey-limits-1: A water journey has no single starting place or fixed travel time.
library-water-journey-limits-2: Try another path and compare what our model includes and leaves out.
library-night-sky-limits: This is an invented sky model, not tonight’s view from Guam, a star finder or a navigation tool. Dots, distances and brightness are symbolic; connecting lines are imagined. Earth’s rotation changes the view over a night, its orbit changes seasonal views, and location changes the visible sky. No Sun-looking or outdoor activity is needed.
library-night-sky-day-1: The marked place faces the Sun in this position.
library-night-sky-day-2: Daylight makes most other stars hard to see, but those stars have not disappeared.
library-night-sky-turn-1: Turn Earth so the marked place faces away from the Sun.
library-night-sky-turn-2: The Sun does not circle our planet to switch the light off.
library-night-sky-night-1: As Earth keeps turning, the stars seem to move across the view.
library-night-sky-night-2: This model changes in chosen steps so you can stop and look.
library-night-sky-pattern-1: Connect a few dots to make an invented shape.
library-night-sky-pattern-2: Real stars are not joined by those lines and can lie at different distances.
library-night-sky-season-1: As Earth orbits the Sun, the night-facing direction changes.
library-night-sky-season-2: Which constellations you can see also depends on your location and the hour.
library-night-sky-limits-1: These star dots do not show today’s date, real directions or exact star positions.
library-night-sky-limits-2: Use the picture to ask questions, not to find your way.
